rationale: Asks who Horace Mann is associated with - identifying the common-school reformer of the Age of Reform.
Identifies Jackson's point of view (the Bank as an undemocratic financial monopoly) as depicted in the 1836 anti-Bank cartoon.
Identifies which group's interests the cartoon shows aligned with the Bank, judging who would oppose Jackson's war on it.
Compares Jackson's Bank War to TR's trust-busting, identifying the pattern of presidents smashing concentrated economic power.
Identifies which provision of the Compromise of 1850 Northerners rejected (the strengthened Fugitive Slave Act).
Identifies the facts of the 1860 election: Democratic split, Lincoln's Southern vote deficit, slavery in the territories.
Identifies the content of Manifest Destiny as providential continental expansion.
Explains why settlers entered Mexican Texas in the 1820s (nearly free land grants) - a causation judgment on motive.
Identifies the Know-Nothing (American) Party as the nativist party of the 1850s political realignment.
Explains the historical significance of Uncle Tom's Cabin (turning Northern opinion against slavery) via the source's purpose and situation.
Explains Stowe's rhetorical purpose in disclaiming 'invidious feeling' - blaming the institution to keep moderate readers from closing the book.
Compares Stowe's sympathy-through-suffering method to abolitionist slave narratives, identifying a shared persuasive technique.
Identifies Northern wartime advantages, recognizing that holding more territory was the one advantage the North lacked.
Identifies why Europe withheld Confederate recognition (alternative cotton, doubtful victory, antislavery after Emancipation).
Explains Northern resentment of the draft through its substitute-and-buy-out provisions ('rich man's war, poor man's fight').
Identifies Vicksburg's strategic payoff: giving the Union control of the Mississippi River.
Identifies the Copperheads as Northern Democrats who opposed the Civil War.
Explains Scott's purpose and point of view from the Anaconda Plan passage (blockade-plus-Mississippi strangulation with less bloodshed).
Identifies the North's decisive material advantage (far greater industrial output and railroad networks).
Identifies the historical situation of Scott's plan - Northern leaders' ridicule of its slowness.
Identifies the Radical Republican program, excluding the restoration of ex-Confederate leaders to power.
Identifies the stated legal ground for Johnson's impeachment (violating the Tenure of Office Act).
Identifies the Black Codes' function: restricting Black movement and barring occupations to bind labor.
Explains the Compromise of 1877's end of Reconstruction via the withdrawal of federal troops (causation).
Identifies the Fifteenth Amendment's content (barring racial discrimination in voting).
Identifies the historical situation making 1876 significant for Bruce's optimistic speech (federal protection of Black rights collapsing as Reconstruction ended).
Identifies the historical context of Reconstruction-era Black officeholding (Black Southerners voted overwhelmingly Republican).
Compares Bruce's patience-and-self-improvement emphasis with Du Bois's demand for immediate civil rights, identifying the sharpest contrast.
Identifies the community mutual-aid strategy that let Plains farmers survive (help from neighboring settlers).
Identifies the Exodusters as Southern Blacks who migrated west to farm in Kansas.
Identifies the Dawes Act's purpose: turning Native Americans into individual farmers via allotment.
Identifies the Populist Party as the organization that gave farmers' views the largest national audience.
Identifies the Turner Thesis's argument: western expansion's effect on the American character.
Explains the federal government's purpose in subsidizing the transcontinental railroad (promoting western settlement).
Identifies the post-Civil War West's defining change: the frontier rapidly disappeared.
Explains farmers' fear of railroads: monopoly freight rates controlled farm profits.
Identifies Taylorism's purpose: maximum efficiency in factory operations (scientific management).
Identifies what drew voters into Gilded Age politics, excluding dynamic presidential candidates.
Explains what Coxey's Army's failure reveals: the era's hands-off federal role in depressions, parallel to Hoover's early-1930s approach.
Identifies features of the industrial city, excluding water-powered factories (steam had replaced water by 1890).
Identifies the best evidence for improving working-class living standards (wage gains measured against living costs).

Identifies the evidential basis of Tarbell's argument (financial data on dividends/profits/capitalization); 2.A is the only 'identify' fit inside the constrained Sourcing parent, though the task is really about the source's evidence.
Identifies what Standard Oil's dominance meant: a handful of men controlling enormous annually-reinvested revenues.
Explains the effect of trust concentration: Progressive antitrust action culminating in the 1911 Standard Oil breakup.
Identifies the Roosevelt Corollary's purposes; imperialism properly belongs to U7 topics 7.2/7.3 but the item is U6, so 6.13 is the forced best fit.
Explains humanitarian support for the Spanish-American War (horror at Spain's reconcentration policy in Cuba); U6-forced topic.
Identifies the chief criticism of the Panama Canal project (underhanded tactics to get canal rights); U6-forced topic.
Explains Hawaii's annexation via the pro-American planters' revolt; U6-forced topic.
Explains missionary support for imperialism (empire as a field for converting new peoples); U6-forced topic.
Identifies what changed Twain's imperialist view (reading the Treaty of Paris); U6-forced topic.
Connects Twain's anti-imperialism to the earlier republican fear that empire corrupts liberty at home; 6.14 is the only U6 topic fitting a continuity claim.
Identifies Twain's central objection (conquest and subjugation, not liberation); U6-forced topic.
Identifies what Progressive reforms achieved, excluding gains for migrant farm workers.
Explains TR's 1912 run as causation: outrage at Taft's Justice Department moving against U.S. Steel.
Identifies why the Wilson years discouraged Black Americans (all three factors true).
Identifies the common ground of Progressives and Socialists: capitalism had created vast inequality.
Identifies who was least likely to be a Progressive (a major U.S. Steel stockholder).
Identifies the Meat Inspection Act's mechanism from the source (continuous federal presence in plants plus a government stamp).
Compares the Meat Inspection Act's approach to the ICC's ongoing railroad supervision, identifying the closest parallel.
Identifies the act's strongest opponents (the meatpacking companies).
Identifies the steps toward war with Germany, excluding the Sussex Pledge (a move away from war).
Explains French opposition to the Fourteen Points (desire to punish Germany, not reform the world).
Identifies home-front mobilization features: celebrities selling Liberty Bonds.
Identifies the critics' argument against Lusitania outrage (munitions aboard, prior sinkings, German warnings).
Explains senatorial opposition to the League (Article X could commit U.S. troops without Congress).
Identifies Lodge's point of view from the 'mongrel banner' passage: contempt for divided international allegiance.
Explains the League campaign's failure: Wilson's refusal to accept Lodge's reservations.
Identifies Lodge's reading of Article X (committing the U.S. to defend other members' territory).
Identifies what rural 1920s America would support: creationism in schools (Scopes-era cultural conflict).
Identifies the novel endorsing 1920s business philosophy (Barton's The Man Nobody Knows).
Identifies the 1928 urban institution: the Prohibition speakeasy.
Identifies Republican 1920s orthodoxy, excluding support for strengthening unions; the content blends economic policy (7.7) and immigration (7.8), so the fit is genuinely split.
Identifies what Hoover's 1928 election showed, excluding the fading of urban-rural divisions.
Identifies the character of Parker's review: a witty demolition of celebrity self-promotion.
Explains the significance of McPherson's prominence: mass media turning preachers into national celebrities.
Identifies the disillusioned 1920s writers' response: expatriation to Paris.
Identifies crash causes, excluding excessive American loans to Europe.
Identifies businessmen's charges against the New Deal (all three true).
Identifies the FDIC's purpose: insuring individual bank deposits.
Identifies which women kept Depression jobs (domestic workers).
Explains the Long/Coughlin phenomenon: Americans demanding the government do more to fight the Depression.
Explains Townsend's economic rationale from the passage: pension money spent immediately would stimulate production.
Explains how Roosevelt related to the Townsend/Long movements: political threats to outflank with his own pension plan.
Compares the Townsend Plan to Huey Long's Share Our Wealth, identifying the parallel populist cash-remedy.
Identifies the real drivers of Japanese-American internment, excluding the official 'protection' pretext.
Identifies the critics' claim about wartime hatred, excluding the Bataan Death March as a from-the-start cause.
Identifies Yalta criticisms, excluding Soviet control of most of Germany; the item is wartime diplomacy shaping the postwar order, so 7.14 edges out 7.13.
Explains U.S. inaction toward Hitler: domestic absorption plus the Nye Committee's anti-interventionism.
Identifies wartime leisure, excluding auto racing (killed by rationing).
Explains Truman's purpose in the Hiroshima press release: announce and justify the revolutionary new weapon.
Identifies Midway's decisiveness: destroying four Japanese carriers.
Identifies the source's notable omission - no mention of the Soviet entry into the war - a limitation framing victory as America's weapon alone.
Identifies what the Army-McCarthy hearings proved: McCarthy had little proof and his support collapsed.
Identifies the containment doctrine: hold firm against Communist expansion worldwide.
Explains U.S. opposition to Communist expansion in Latin America: deep American economic interests there.
Identifies HUAC's Hollywood targets (all three groups true).
Identifies the 'soft on communism' charges, excluding the loyalty-program claim (Truman created the federal loyalty system).
Identifies from Bentley's testimony what her Soviet contacts obtained (aircraft-production intelligence, including D-Day).
Explains how spy revelations related to congressional action: passage of internal-security laws such as the McCarran Act.
Compares HUAC's investigations to the Palmer Raids, identifying the shared anti-radical precedent.
Identifies 1950s consumer-spending drivers, excluding a rush to buy stocks.
Identifies the presidency most resembling Eisenhower's: Coolidge's pro-business fiscal conservatism.
Identifies how Depression and war shaped 1950s families: turning inward to family and giving children what they had lacked.
Identifies early-1950s television's deepest impact: imposing social conformity.
Explains the fear of rock 'n' roll: its Black roots and many Black musicians.
Identifies Spock's departure from earlier experts: urging parents to trust natural instincts over rigid schedules.
Explains the significance of Spock's guidance as the postwar expert culture of child psychology shaping family life.
Compares Spock's trusted-expert role to Julia Child's mass-media instruction of suburban homemakers.
Explains what the Freedom Riders' fate revealed: neither Washington nor the states were yet committed protectors of civil rights workers.
Explains what Tet demonstrated: officials had not been candid about the war.
Identifies when SDS membership peaked: the 1965-67 draft escalation.
Identifies Black Power's Northern appeal, excluding mass membership in the Nation of Islam.
Identifies feminist highlights of the era, excluding ERA ratification (never achieved).
Identifies Carmichael's meaning of Black Power: Black people's right to define their own goals without white approval.
Identifies what Black Power broke with: the nonviolent, integrationist civil rights mainstream.
Compares Carmichael's self-definition emphasis to Marcus Garvey's Black nationalism, identifying the continued tradition.
Identifies Nixon's 1972 campaign tactics, excluding falsifying opponents' war records.
Identifies supply-side claims, excluding increased savings; a Reagan-era topic forced into the U8 economy code.
Identifies Reagan-deficit contributors, excluding education funding; a Reagan-era topic forced into the U8 economy code.
Identifies Reagan critics' emphasis: his policies' effects on the middle and lower classes.
Explains what Ford's WIN program convinced Americans: that he had no real grasp of economics.
Identifies Reagan's argument from the passage: raising taxes encourages spending and destroys jobs.
Explains critics' prediction about Reagan's tax cuts: they would explode the federal deficit.
Identifies Reagan's break with detente: confrontation and military superiority rather than accommodation.
Identifies Clinton's defining characteristic: pragmatic, centrist policymaking.
Explains Bush's alienation of conservatives: breaking the 'no new taxes' pledge in the 1990 deficit deal.
Identifies the 'vision thing': Bush never defined America's post-Cold War role.
Identifies factors ending the Cold War, excluding arms makers' desire to end the arms race.
Identifies Clinton's strengths vs. Republicans, excluding winning over the New Right.
Identifies Greenspan's central question: how to tell when asset prices have become dangerously inflated.
Explains how Greenspan's 'irrational exuberance' warning related to a later development: the dot-com crash of 2000-2001.
Compares Greenspan's 1996 bubble worry to the 1920s Fed's failure to restrain speculation.
Identifies Bush's stated Iraq War reasons, excluding the assassination-plot claim.
Identifies religious-right goals, excluding income-tax cuts for the wealthy.
Identifies Obama's most significant legislative achievement: the Affordable Care Act.
Identifies what hurt Kerry in 2004, excluding his debate performance.
Compares Bush's democracy-spreading drive to Wilson's Fourteen Points idealism.
Identifies Giuliani's central claim: no cause can justify terrorism against innocent civilians.
Explains how Congress responded to 9/11: authorizing military force against those responsible.
Identifies Congress's legislative response to 9/11: the USA Patriot Act.
Identifies the Obama foreign-policy initiative Trump vowed to overturn: the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA).
Identifies the collusion accusation against Trump's campaign: Russia.
Identifies the country receiving Biden's military and diplomatic support: Ukraine.
Compares Trump's anti-establishment populism to Andrew Jackson's.
Compares the COVID-19 pandemic to the Spanish Flu of 1918.
Identifies how Trump frames the fight against extremism: a shared battle of good against evil uniting all faiths.
Identifies where the Trump administration took military action against terrorists: Syria.
Identifies the longer-term approach Trump's Arab outreach continued: relying on regional partnerships to advance American interests.
Identifies from Addams's account the striking girls' vulnerability: dependence on employers and landlords for housing.
Identifies settlement houses' function as meeting places where workers could organize, illustrated by Hull House in the shoe-factory strike.
